content.title: 2. BACKGROUND AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
content.narrative_summary: This section describes the epidemiology of atrial fibrillation (AF), noting it is the most common sustained arrhythmia with rising global incidence and prevalence due to population aging, obesity, improved detection, and survival with cardiovascular disease. The estimated global prevalence was 50 million in 2020; in 2015, about 11% of U.S. AF cases were undiagnosed. AF is linked to higher healthcare utilization and costs: insured patients with incident AF had a 2.41‐fold higher risk of inpatient and cardiovascular ED visits, and annual health care costs of $63 031 versus $35 896 for those without AF. In 2016, AF accounted for $28.4 billion in U.S. healthcare spending. U.S. AF prevalence was 5.2 million in 2010 (projected 12.1 million by 2030), with incidence rising from 1.2 million cases in 2010 to an expected 2.6 million.

It reports overall lifetime risk (~30–40% in White, ~20% in African American, ~15% in Chinese individuals). AF is associated with 1.5–2-fold increased risk of death, higher mortality risk in women, and, in meta-analyses, increased risks of stroke (2.4-fold), cognitive impairment or dementia (1.5-fold), myocardial infarction (1.5-fold), sudden cardiac death (2-fold), heart failure (5-fold), chronic kidney disease (1.6-fold), and peripheral artery disease (1.3-fold). Among Medicare beneficiaries, 5-year outcomes after AF diagnosis include death (19.5% at 1 year; 48.8% at 5 years), heart failure (13.7%), new-onset stroke (7.1%), gastrointestinal hemorrhage (5.7%), and myocardial infarction (3.9%).

content.narrative_summary: The page continues a discussion of CTI-dependent atrial flutter, describing it as a macroreentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus with typical and reverse typical forms and noting that this terminology is no longer used. section_headings: 2.3.2 Atrial Structural Abnormalities, Remodeling, and Atrial Myopathy
content.narrative_summary: This section describes mechanisms by which atrial fibrillation (AF) is initiated and sustained, including ectopic firing from pulmonary veins, electrophysiological remodeling (perturbations in Ca2+ handling, ion currents, connexin remodeling), and resulting triggers such as premature atrial contractions linked to AF onset. It also introduces atrial structural abnormalities and myopathy—fibrosis, collagen deposition, altered ion channel expression, inflammation—and outlines upstream pathways (inflammatory, oxidative stress, RAAS activation, calcium overload) that increase AF susceptibility.

section_headings: 2.3.3. Role of the Autonomic Nervous System
content.narrative_summary: This page continues discussion of upstream therapies, describing the RAAS regulation of blood pressure and obesity (vascular smooth muscle constriction, fibroblast activation, increased reactive oxygen species) and attenuation of pathologic changes with ACE inhibitors or angiotensin-II receptor blockers. It details oxidative stress mechanisms including activation of CaMKII and JNK leading to calcium overload, increased late sodium current (I_Na,L), reactive lipid products, NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, mitochondrial/metabolic stress, inflammatory changes, and myofilament degradation. Systemic inflammatory activation and the role of the NLRP3 inflammasome in AF pathophysiology are noted (NLRP3 knockdown prevented AF in a mouse model). Persistence of AF is linked to substrate properties (short refractory period × conduction velocity in fibrotic/fatty atria). It introduces the autonomic nervous system as both trigger and substrate for AF (see Figure 8).

section_headings: 2.5 Addressing Health Inequities and Barriers to AF Management
content.narrative_summary: Under “ANS triggers AF,” the guideline reviews how sympathetic and parasympathetic efferent stimulation—via noradrenaline release, β-adrenergic receptor activation, L-type calcium channel enhancement, inward current increases, delayed afterdepolarization (ryanodine-2 dysfunction), and parasympathetic IKACh activity—can initiate atrial fibrillation. “ANS maintains AF” outlines how atrial hyperinnervation, electrical fractionation, afferent reflex deficiencies, volume and pressure homeostasis disruption, and anatomic remodeling contribute to AF perpetuation. Section 2.4 “Genetics” describes heritability of common and familial AF, GWAS identifying over 100 loci, findings from UK Biobank and NHLBI Trans Omics on TTN loss-of-function and other cardiomyopathy/arrhythmia gene variants (TTN, MYH7, MYH6, LMNA, KCNQ1), and age- and ancestry-related variant prevalence.

content.narrative_summary: This section describes risk prediction models for incident atrial fibrillation (AF) in the community, noting over 20 models. content.title: Basic Evaluation
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis emphasizes that initial evaluation of newly diagnosed or suspected atrial fibrillation should confirm the diagnosis, identify clinical factors impacting management, and include targeted history, physical examination, ECG for electrical substrates, basic laboratory tests for disorders affecting stroke and bleeding risk, and transthoracic echocardiography for chamber size, function, and valvular pathology. Echocardiography provides information on left atrial size and compliance associated with AF progression, while laboratory testing detects conditions such as chronic kidney disease, liver dysfunction, and hyperthyroidism, guiding therapeutic decisions. Recommendation‐specific supportive text details that echocardiography is essential for evaluating chamber and valve function, right ventricular pressure, and left ventricular ejection fraction for rhythm therapy decisions, and that AF alone should not prompt routine protocolized testing for ischemia, ACS, or PE in the absence of signs or symptoms, based on retrospective analyses.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Basic Clinical Evaluation

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with newly diagnosed AF, a transthoracic echocardiogram¹⁻⁴ to assess cardiac structure, laboratory testing to include a complete blood count, metabolic panel, and thyroid function,⁵⁻⁷ and when clinical suspicion exists, targeted testing to assess for other medical conditions associated with AF are recommended to determine stroke and bleeding risk factors, as well as underlying conditions that will guide further management.

2. In patients with newly diagnosed AF, protocolized testing for ischemia, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and pulmonary embolism (PE) should not routinely be performed to assess the etiology of AF unless there are additional signs or symptoms to indicate those disorders.⁸⁻¹⁰

content.title: 4.2.2. Rhythm Monitoring Tools and Methods
content.narrative_summary: The page outlines rhythm monitoring options for atrial fibrillation, including standard 12-lead ECG, loop recorders, implantable cardiac monitors, pacemakers/defibrillators with atrial leads, handheld ECGs, and smartwatches with photoplethysmography. It highlights that initial AF diagnosis should rely on clinician interpretation due to algorithm limitations; implantable monitors offer highest sensitivity; and algorithms can estimate AF burden but require periodic human review. A recommendation-specific text begins to detail these points but is incomplete at page end.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Rhythm Monitoring Tools and Methods

rows.recommendation: Among individuals without a known history of AF, it is recommended that an initial AF diagnosis be made by a clinician using visual interpretation of the electrocardiographic signals, regardless of the type of rhythm or monitoring device.¹⁻⁵

In patients with an intracardiac rhythm device capable of a diagnosis of AF, such as from an atrial pacemaker lead, a diagnosis of AF should only be made after it is visually confirmed by reviewing intracardiac tracings to exclude signal artifacts and other arrhythmias.⁶⁻⁹
For patients who have had a systemic thromboembolic event without a known history of AF and in whom maximum sensitivity to detect AF is sought, an implantable cardiac monitor is reasonable.¹⁰,¹¹

Among patients with a diagnosis of AF, it is reasonable to infer AF frequency, duration, and burden using automated algorithms available from electrocardiographic monitors, implantable cardiac monitors, and cardiac rhythm devices with an atrial lead, recognizing that periodic review can be required to exclude other arrhythmias.¹,⁴,⁵,¹²

Among patients with AF in whom cardiac monitoring is advised, it is reasonable to recommend use of a consumer-accessible electrocardiographic device that provides a high-quality tracing to detect recurrences.¹³

content.title: 2023 Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation
content.narrative_summary: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) have a variably increased risk of stroke, and several clinical risk scores (eg, CHA₂DS₂-VASc, ATRIA, GARFIELD-AF) have been developed and validated to discriminate low (<1%/y), intermediate (~1–2%/y), and high (>2%/y) annual stroke risk. These scores should be calibrated and validated in the target population to ensure accurate, unbiased risk prediction. Bleeding risk assessments should consider predictors of both stroke and bleeding to balance the benefits and risks of anticoagulation. Incorporating additional predictors can improve discrimination, but absolute risk associated with specific score levels varies across populations.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Risk Stratification Schemes

rows.recommendation: 1. Patients with AF should be evaluated for their annual risk of thromboembolic events using a validated clinical risk score, such as CHA₂DS₂-VASc.¹⁻⁴

2. Patients with AF should be evaluated for factors that specifically indicate a higher risk of bleeding, such as previous bleeding and use of drugs that increase bleeding risk, in order to identify possible interventions to prevent bleeding on anticoagulation.⁵⁻⁷

3. Patients with AF at intermediate annual risk of thromboembolic events by risk scores (eg, equivalent to CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 1 in men or 2 in women), who remain uncertain about the benefit of anticoagulation, can benefit from consideration of factors that might modify their risk of stroke to help inform the decision.*
rows.supporting_text: *Factors may include AF burden or other features in Table 3.

rows.recommendation: 4. In patients who are deemed at high risk for stroke, bleeding risk scores should not be used in isolation to determine eligibility for oral anticoagulation but instead to identify and modify bleeding risk factors and to inform medical decision-making.⁸⁻¹⁰

content.narrative_summary: The text continues a discussion of stroke risk scores in atrial fibrillation. It notes that a CHA₂DS₂‐VASc score of 2 corresponds to annual stroke rates of <1% in 4 cohorts, 1–2% in 6 cohorts, and >2% in 5 cohorts (Figure 9). CHA₂DS₂‐VASc is the most validated and preferred score despite suboptimal performance in populations such as those with renal disease, prompting development of newer scores like ATRIA and GARFIELD-AF which modestly improve discrimination but lack rigorous calibration evaluation. A meta-analysis reported 19 risk scores, 329 external validations, and 76 updates. Potential differences among the most studied risk scores are listed in Table 9. The GARFIELD-AF score may offer advantages by including mortality and bleeding risk to facilitate comprehensive patient discussions and additional variables such as smoking status, renal disease, and dementia. The guideline does not preclude future development of more accurate stratification scores. Clinical decisions on stroke prevention must balance ischemic stroke risk, bleeding risk, net clinical benefit, and patient preferences, noting that HAS-BLED, HEMORR₂HAGES, and ATRIA discriminate poorly between patients.

In patients with AF at risk for stroke, reevaluation of the need for and choice of stroke risk reduction therapy at periodic intervals is recommended to reassess stroke and bleeding risk, net clinical benefit, and proper dosing.

content.title: 6.3 Oral Anticoagulants
content.narrative_summary: Warfarin has been used since the 1950s as first‐line oral anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation but is limited by a narrow therapeutic window (INR 2–3), frequent monitoring, CYP2C9‐mediated drug interactions, dietary restrictions, and cost. Despite these issues, warfarin remains appropriate in patients who cannot afford or use DOACs, and in those with moderate to severe rheumatic mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valves. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) were developed to address warfarin’s disadvantages and are recommended as first‐line therapy in AF, except…

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Antithrombotic Therapy

rows.recommendation: 1. For patients with AF and an estimated annual thromboembolic risk of ≥2% per year (eg, CHA2DS2‐VASc score of ≥2 in men and ≥3 in women), anticoagulation is recommended to prevent stroke and systemic thromboembolism.

2. In patients with AF who do not have a history of moderate to severe rheumatic mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve, and who are candidates for anticoagulation, DOACs are recommended over warfarin to reduce the risk of mortality, stroke, systemic embolism, and ICH.

3. For patients with AF and an estimated annual thromboembolic risk of ≥1% but <2% per year (equivalent to CHA2DS2‐VASc score of 1 in men and 2 in women), anticoagulation is reasonable to prevent stroke and systemic thromboembolism.

4. In patients with AF who are candidates for anticoagulation and without an indication for antiplatelet therapy, aspirin either alone or in combination with clopidogrel as an alternative to anticoagulation is not recommended to reduce stroke risk.
5. In patients with AF without risk factors for stroke, aspirin monotherapy for prevention of thromboembolic events is of no benefit.

content.title: 6.3.1.1. Considerations in Managing Anticoagulants
content.narrative_summary: Multiple factors, including efficacy, safety, insurance coverage, renal/hepatic function, drug interaction screening, medication adherence, and patient preferences, inform selection of optimal oral anticoagulant therapy in patients with AF. Dosing of DOACs should account for age, renal function, weight, hepatic function, and concomitant medications. Strong CYP3A4 and/or p-glycoprotein inhibitors (eg, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir) and inducers (eg, rifampin, phenytoin, St. John’s wort) significantly alter DOAC plasma levels and risk of bleeding or thromboembolism. Routine measurement of DOAC concentrations is generally not indicated except in select clinical scenarios (eg, before invasive procedures or to assess adherence). If warfarin is chosen over DOACs, achieving and maintaining a higher time in therapeutic INR range (≥70%) with consistent vitamin K intake, thorough monitoring, and patient education is important.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Considerations in Managing Anticoagulants

rows.recommendation: For patients with AF receiving DOACs, optimal management of drug interactions is recommended for those receiving concomitant therapy with interacting drugs, especially CYP3A4 and/or p-glycoprotein inhibitors or inducers (Table 13).1-7

For patients with AF receiving warfarin,* a target INR between 2 and 3 is recommended, as well as optimal management of drug-drug interactions, consistency in vitamin K dietary intake, and routine INR monitoring to improve time in therapeutic range and to minimize risks of preventable thromboembolism or major bleeding.8-10
For patients with AF, nonevidence-based doses of DOACs should be avoided to minimize risks of preventable thromboembolism or major bleeding and to improve survival.11,12

content.narrative_summary: This page provides trial‐specific supportive evidence for surgical left atrial appendage occlusion (S-LAAO). It describes the LAAOS III randomized trial (4,770 patients with AF and CHAD2DS2-VASc ≥2) showing a 33% reduction in stroke and systemic embolism with adjunctive S-LAAO plus oral anticoagulation versus no S-LAAO. Ongoing evidence gaps include variable occlusion methods, inconsistent reporting of occlusion success, and the need for further RCTs.

content.title: Active Bleeding on Anticoagulant Therapy and Reversal Drugs
section_headings: 6.6 Active Bleeding on Anticoagulant Therapy and Reversal Drugs
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: About 2% to 4% of patients on oral anticoagulants experience major bleeding requiring intervention. Activated charcoal may be administered up to 6 to 8 hours after the last dose of a DOAC; hemodialysis may be considered for dabigatran removal but is challenging due to coagulation and hemodynamic instability. FDA-approved reversal agents include idarucizumab for dabigatran and andexanet alfa or four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) for factor Xa inhibitors; four-factor PCC is preferred for VKA-induced bleeding. Recommendation-Supportive Text: The RE-VERSE AD study showed idarucizumab reversed dabigatran anticoagulation in 100% of patients with uncontrolled or life-threatening bleeding (67.7% hemostasis; 4.7% thrombosis rate at 30 days). A post hoc analysis in gastrointestinal bleeding found 97.5% complete reversal and 76.2% bleeding cessation. Data on PCC for dabigatran-associated bleeding are very limited.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Active Bleeding on Anticoagulant Therapy and Reversal Drugs

rows.recommendation: In patients with AF receiving dabigatran who develop life-threatening bleeding, treatment with idarucizumab is recommended to rapidly reverse dabigatran’s anticoagulation effect.¹-³

In patients with AF receiving dabigatran who develop life-threatening bleeding, treatment with activated prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is reasonable to reverse dabigatran’s anticoagulation effect if idarucizumab is unavailable.⁴,⁵

In patients with AF receiving factor Xa inhibitors who develop life-threatening bleeding, treatment with either andexanet alfa (apixaban or rivaroxaban,* edoxaban†) or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate† is recommended to rapidly reverse factor Xa inhibitor’s anticoagulation effect.⁶,⁷
rows.supporting_text: *B-NR LOE applies to data on apixaban or rivaroxaban; †C-LD LOE applies to data on edoxaban.

rows.recommendation: In patients with AF receiving warfarin who develop life-threatening bleeding, treatment with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (if available) in addition to intravenous vitamin K is recommended to rapidly achieve INR correction over fresh frozen plasma and intravenous vitamin K treatment.⁸-¹⁰

section_headings: 6.6.1. Management of Patients With AF and ICH
content.narrative_summary: The page continues a discussion of meta-analyses comparing reversal strategies for factor Xa inhibitor–associated bleeding and optimal timing for resuming anticoagulation after gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). rows.recommendation: In patients with AF and conditions associated with very high risk of thromboembolic events (>5%/year), such as rheumatic heart disease or a mechanical heart valve, early (1–2 weeks) resumption of anticoagulation after ICH is reasonable to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events.

In patients with AF and conditions associated with high risk of recurrent ICH (eg, cerebral amyloid angiopathy), anticoagulation-sparing strategies (eg, LAAO) may be considered to reduce the risk of recurrent hemorrhage.

content.title: 6.7. Periprocedural Management
content.narrative_summary: Continues discussion of resuming oral anticoagulation after intracerebral hemorrhage, noting median resumption times, associated risks of ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, and mortality with DOACs versus VKAs, and alternative stroke prevention strategies such as left atrial appendage closure or epicardial clipping in patients with atrial fibrillation and cerebral amyloid angiopathy. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Periprocedural Management

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with AF (excluding those with recent stroke or TIA, or a mechanical valve) and on oral anticoagulation with either warfarin* or DOAC† who are scheduled to undergo an invasive procedure or surgery, temporary cessation of oral anticoagulation without bridging anticoagulation is recommended.

2. In patients with AF on warfarin anticoagulation and an annual predicted risk of thromboembolism of ≥5% undergoing pacemaker or defibrillator implantation or generator change, continued anticoagulation is recommended in preference to interruption of warfarin and bridging anticoagulation with heparin to reduce the risk of pocket hematoma.

3. In patients with AF with CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 or equivalent risk of stroke, on DOAC anticoagulation and undergoing pacemaker or defibrillator implantation or generator change, either uninterrupted or interrupted DOAC is reasonable.

4. In patients with AF on DOAC and scheduled to undergo an invasive procedure or surgery that cannot be performed safely on uninterrupted anticoagulation, the timing of interruption of DOAC should be guided by the specific agent, renal function, and the bleeding risk of the procedure (Table 18).

5. In patients with AF on DOAC that has been interrupted for an invasive procedure or surgery, in general, resumption of anticoagulation the day after low bleeding risk surgery and between the evening of the second day and the evening of the third day after high bleeding risk surgery is reasonable, as long as hemostasis has been achieved and further bleeding is not anticipated.

6. In patients with AF on warfarin anticoagulation, who are undergoing surgeries or procedures for which they are holding warfarin, except in patients with mechanical valve or recent stroke or TIA, bridging anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin should not be administered.

content.narrative_summary: This page continues the discussion of balancing bleeding and thrombotic risk when interrupting anticoagulation for invasive procedures. Procedures are stratified into low and high bleeding risk based on type (eg, dental and ophthalmologic versus neurosurgical or cardiac). content.title: 6.8.4. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)/Kidney Failure
content.narrative_summary: Chronic kidney disease independently increases stroke risk in atrial fibrillation (AF) patients, particularly in those on dialysis. Evidence is conflicting regarding stroke rates in dialysis cohorts due to factors such as underdiagnosed AF and anticoagulation removal by hemodialysis. Vitamin K antagonists have reduced time in therapeutic range and are substantially removed by dialysis. Pivotal DOAC trials excluded dialysis patients; pharmacokinetic data guide dosing. Early studies suggest varied bleeding and thromboembolism outcomes with dabigatran and rivaroxaban. Data on LAAO and prospective anticoagulation comparisons in this population are limited.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for CKD/Kidney Failure

rows.recommendation: 1. For patients with AF at elevated risk for stroke and CKD stage 3, treatment with warfarin or, preferably, evidence-based doses of direct thrombin or factor Xa inhibitors (Table 19) is recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.
2. For patients with AF at elevated risk for stroke and CKD stage 4, treatment with warfarin or labeled doses of DOACs is reasonable to reduce the risk of stroke.

3. For patients with AF at elevated risk for stroke and who have end-stage CKD (CrCl <15 mL/min) or are on dialysis, it might be reasonable to prescribe warfarin (INR 2.0–3.0) or an evidence-based dose of apixaban for oral anticoagulation to reduce the risk of stroke.

content.title: Anticoagulation for Typical (CTI-Dependent) AFL
content.narrative_summary: Paragraph 1: Typical atrial flutter (AFL) carries an increased thromboembolic risk compared to the general population (4.1% vs. 1.2% stroke rate) though oral anticoagulation benefit is difficult to isolate when AFL and atrial fibrillation coexist. Transesophageal echocardiography after AFL ablation shows left atrial thrombus or spontaneous contrast in a small proportion (3%). Thromboembolic event rates with cardioversion range from 0% to 6%, highest within 1 to 2 days postprocedure. Echocardiographic studies report left atrial thrombus in 0%–38% and spontaneous contrast in 21%–28% of cases. Paragraph 2: The incidence of embolism after cardioversion of AFL (0.72%) is similar to atrial fibrillation (0.46%), and left atrial appendage (LAA) stunning contributes to thrombus formation postconversion. Continued anticoagulation is recommended early after cardioversion to sinus rhythm.

Although acute procedural success rates exceed 90%, subsequent AF occurrence varies (16–82%), warranting close follow-up and monitoring. Predictors of AF after flutter ablation include LA enlargement, inducible AF, prolonged interatrial conduction, HV interval, COPD, sleep apnea, and HATCH score. Even with successful ablation, patients remain at risk of new-onset AF and thromboembolic events. The page then introduces Rate Control strategies. content.narrative_summary: Paragraph 4: Intravenous amiodarone effectively controls ventricular rate in critically ill AF patients. In a retrospective study of 38 ICU patients, it achieved a significant heart rate decrease without BP reduction compared with IV diltiazem and digoxin. A separate randomized study of 60 AF patients with HR >120 bpm compared three regimens (diltiazem bolus plus infusion, amiodarone 300 mg bolus, and amiodarone 300 mg bolus plus infusion) and found similar >30% rate reductions within 4 hours but a higher incidence of hypotension requiring discontinuation in the amiodarone-only group. Retrospective analyses associate diltiazem use in AF with RVR and LVEF ≤50% with increased acute kidney injury (10% vs. 3.6%; P=0.002) and higher rates of worsened HF symptoms compared with metoprolol or norm EF, without differences in mortality, level of care, or hypotension.

content.title: 7.2.2. Long-Term Rate Control
content.narrative_summary: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil and diltiazem) and beta blockers are effective for long-term rate control in AF, particularly in the absence of preexcitation. Digoxin may be useful in patients with limited tolerability to other agents or as adjunct therapy in those with difficult-to-control ventricular rates. Limited comparative data exist, and selection of specific agents should consider patient-specific factors (eg, HFrEF, reactive airway disease) and individual response.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Long-Term Rate Control

rows.recommendation: In patients with AF, beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are recommended for long-term rate control with the choice of agent according to underlying substrate and comorbid conditions.
For patients with AF in whom measuring serum digoxin levels is indicated, it is reasonable to target levels <1.2 ng/mL.

In patients with AF and HF symptoms, digoxin is reasonable for long-term rate control in combination with other rate-controlling agents, or as monotherapy if other agents are not preferred, not tolerated, or contraindicated.
In patients with AF and LVEF <40%, nondihydropyridine calcium channel-blocking drugs should not be administered given their potential to exacerbate HF.
In patients with permanent AF who have risk factors for cardiovascular events, dronedarone should not be used for long-term rate control.

content.title: Atrioventricular Nodal Ablation (AVNA)
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that while AVNA effectively controls ventricular rate without medications, it creates pacemaker dependence. Small RCTs and right ventricular pacing improve symptoms and quality of life but do not affect ejection fraction or other measures of cardiac performance. Antiarrhythmic drugs reduce transition to permanent AF but do not improve QOL and may increase HF and hospitalizations. Early concerns regarding malignant arrhythmias post-AVNA have been minimized by higher lower-rate pacing protocols, with subsequent rate adjustments over several weeks. Long-term data are limited, and no evidence supports AVNA as first-line therapy. The recommendation-specific supportive text notes a 3% to 7% incidence of sudden death after AVNA due to ventricular fibrillation related to bradycardia, QT prolongation, and repolarization heterogeneity, which has been mitigated by higher initial pacing rates. It also highlights that AVNA with pacemaker implantation provides safe and effective rate control and symptom relief in patients unresponsive to medical therapy, though without survival or ejection fraction benefit and with nonnegligible complication rates.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for AVNA

rows.recommendation: In patients with AF and a persistently rapid ventricular response who undergo AVNA, initial pacemaker lower rate programming should be 80 to 90 bpm to reduce the risk of sudden death.

In patients with AF and uncontrolled rapid ventricular response refractory to rate-control medications (who are not candidates for or in whom rhythm control has been unsuccessful), AVNA can be useful to improve symptoms and QOL.

In patients with AF who are planned to undergo AVNA, implantation of a pacemaker before the ablation (ie, before or same day of ablation) is recommended to ensure adequacy of the pacing leads before performing ablation.
In patients with AF with normal EF undergoing AVNA, conduction system pacing of the His bundle or left bundle area may be reasonable.

section_headings: 8.1. Goals of Therapy With Rhythm Control
content.narrative_summary: The page continues a discussion of atrioventricular nodal ablation (AVNA) and pacemaker implantation, noting a 2% overall risk of lead dislodgement, practice variation in timing of AVNA relative to implantation, and higher complication rates in older patients. Conduction system pacing (His bundle or left bundle area) is described as an emerging strategy to reduce RV pacing–induced cardiomyopathy and improve outcomes, particularly in HF patients with reduced or preserved ejection fraction.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Goals of Therapy With Rhythm Control

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with reduced LV function and persistent (or high burden) AF, a trial of rhythm control should be recommended to evaluate whether AF is contributing to the reduced LV function.
2. In patients with symptomatic AF, rhythm control can be useful to improve symptoms.
3. In patients with a recent diagnosis of AF (<1 year), rhythm control can be useful to reduce hospitalizations, stroke, and mortality.
4. In patients with AF and HF, rhythm control can be useful for improving symptoms and improving outcomes, such as mortality and hospitalizations for HF and ischemia.
5. In patients with AF, rhythm-control strategies can be useful to reduce the likelihood of AF progression.

6. In patients with AF where symptoms associated with AF are uncertain, a trial of rhythm control (eg, cardioversion or pharmacological therapy) may be useful to determine what if any symptoms are attributable to AF.
7. In patients with AF, rhythm-control strategies may be useful to reduce the likelihood of development of dementia or worsening cardiac structural abnormalities.

content.narrative_summary: The page begins with a Synopsis summarizing the nuanced decision between rhythm and rate control in atrial fibrillation (AF), citing EAST-AFNET 4 and registry data to emphasize early rhythm control and ongoing risk factor management. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text provides numbered evidence for specific guideline recommendations: (1) the link between AF and reduced left ventricular (LV) function and improvement after sinus rhythm restoration; (2) symptom and quality-of-life benefits of rhythm over rate control and findings from the RACE II study; (3) reduced mortality, stroke, and hospitalization with early rhythm control in EAST-AFNET 4 and observational cohorts; and (4) outcomes from the AF-CHF and CABANA trials demonstrating improved quality of life, mortality reduction, and maintenance of sinus rhythm with rhythm control and catheter ablation.

content.narrative_summary: Figure 19 presents considerations for choosing between rhythm control and rate control, displaying factors grouped under Patient Factors and Physical Examination/Anatomy across three preference categories: Favors Rate Control, Variable, and Favors Rhythm Control. Below the figure, narrative text discusses that the benefit of rhythm control in patients with heart failure is likely greatest in those with recently identified AF, that AF often progresses to higher burdens over time, and that large registry studies report more AF progression with rate-control strategies over a 1–2-year period.

content.narrative_summary: Registry studies show progression to a more sustained AF burden in 26%–28% of patients on a rate-control strategy versus 6%–11% with a rhythm-control strategy; in the ORBIT AF trial, rhythm control was associated with a lower likelihood of progression, but progression remained common (66% for rate control, 56% for rhythm control), influenced by factors such as age and presence of heart failure or other comorbidities including LA size, heart rate, and modifiable risk factors. The reported prevalence of asymptomatic AF varies from 10% to 40%, with asymptomatic and symptomatic patients having similar risks of death and stroke; a post hoc analysis of EAST-AFNET 4 showed similar magnitudes of benefit in both groups for reducing cardiovascular death, stroke, and hospitalization for heart failure. The evidence base for rhythm-control trials in asymptomatic patients with sinus rhythm is limited.

section_headings: 8.2.1. Prevention of Thromboembolism in the Setting of Cardioversion
content.narrative_summary: The section describes cardioversion as an acute rhythm control strategy, achievable electrically or pharmacologically, noting electrical cardioversion’s greater efficacy but also its anesthesia and sedation trade-offs. Thromboembolic risks apply to both methods, and anti-coagulation considerations are introduced for patients undergoing cardioversion.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Prevention of Thromboembolism in the Setting of Cardioversion

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with AF duration of ≥48 hours, a 3-week duration of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation or imaging evaluation to exclude intracardiac thrombus is recommended before elective cardioversion.

2. In patients with AF undergoing cardioversion, therapeutic anticoagulation should be established before cardioversion and continued for at least 4 weeks afterwards without interruption to prevent thromboembolism.

3. In patients with AF in whom cardioversion is deferred due to LAA thrombus detected on pre-cardioversion imaging, therapeutic anticoagulation should be instituted for at least 3 to 6 weeks, after which imaging should be repeated before cardioversion.

4. In patients with AF and previous LAAO who are not on anticoagulation, imaging evaluation to assess the adequacy of LAAO and exclude device-related thrombosis before cardioversion may be reasonable.
5. In patients with AF and previous LAAO with residual leak, peri-cardioversion anticoagulation may be considered and continued thereafter.

6. In patients with reported AF duration of <48 hours (not in the setting of cardiac surgery) and who are not on anticoagulation, precardioversion imaging to exclude intracardiac thrombus may be considered in those who are at elevated thromboembolic risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc score ≥2 or equivalent).

7. In patients with low thromboembolic risks (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 0-1 or equivalent) and AF duration of <12 hours, the benefit of precardioversion imaging or peri-cardioversion anticoagulation is uncertain given the low incidence of pericardioversion thromboembolic events in this population.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis discusses thromboembolic risks associated with pharmacological and electrical cardioversion in atrial fibrillation, highlighting DOACs as alternatives to VKAs, the role of precardioversion imaging (especially in patients with prior LAAO), and the variability of thromboembolic risk based on patient-specific factors such as risk scores and AF duration. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Electrical Cardioversion

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with hemodynamic instability attributable to AF, immediate electrical cardioversion should be performed to restore sinus rhythm.¹
2. In patients with AF who are hemodynamically stable, electrical cardioversion can be performed as initial rhythm-control strategy or after unsuccessful pharmacological cardioversion.²
3. In patients with AF undergoing electrical cardioversion, energy delivery should be confirmed to be synchronized to the QRS to reduce the risk of inducing VF.³

4. For patients with AF undergoing elective electrical cardioversion, the use of biphasic energy of at least 200 J as initial energy can be beneficial to improve success of initial electrical shock.⁴⁻⁵

5. In patients with AF undergoing elective cardioversion, with longer duration of AF or unsuccessful initial shock, optimization of electrode vector, use of higher energy, and pretreatment with antiarrhythmic drugs can facilitate success of electrical cardioversion.⁵⁻⁹
6. In patients with obesity and AF, use of manual pressure augmentation and/or further escalation of electrical energy may be beneficial to improve success of electrical cardioversion.¹⁰

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Pharmacological Cardioversion

rows.recommendation: For patients with AF, pharmacological cardioversion is reasonable as an alternative to electrical cardioversion for those who are hemodynamically stable or in situations when electrical cardioversion is preferred but cannot be performed.
For patients with AF, ibutilide is reasonable for pharmacological cardioversion for patients without depressed LV function (LVEF <40%).
For patients with AF, intravenous amiodarone is reasonable for pharmacological cardioversion, although time to conversion is generally longer than with other agents (8–12 hours).

For patients with recurrent AF occurring outside the setting of a hospital, the “pill-in-the-pocket” (PITP) approach with a single oral dose of flecainide or propafenone, with a concomitant atrioventricular nodal blocking agent, is reasonable for pharmacological cardioversion if previously tested in a monitored setting.
For patients with AF, use of intravenous procainamide may be considered for pharmacological cardioversion when other intravenous agents are contraindicated or not preferred.

content.title: Antiarrhythmic Drugs for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
section_headings: 8.3. Antiarrhythmic Drugs for Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
8.3.1. Specific Drug Therapy for Long-Term Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm
content.narrative_summary: The page begins mid-discussion noting that intravenous procainamide is less effective than ibutilide for conversion of AF to sinus rhythm and is associated with a higher incidence of hypotension and potential exacerbation of HFrEF. The synopsis summarizes that antiarrhythmic drugs are reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm in AF patients who decline or are not candidates for ablation, with options including flecainide, propafenone, dronedarone, dofetilide, sotalol, and low-dose amiodarone. Drug selection should account for structural heart disease, renal function, electrolyte levels, QT interval monitoring, and potential adverse effects, reserving higher-risk agents for situations in which other strategies are ineffective or contraindicated.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Specific Drug Therapy for Long-Term Maintenance of Sinus Rhythm

rows.recommendation: 1. For patients with AF and HFrEF (≤40%), therapy with dofetilide*1 or amiodarone†2 is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm.

2. For patients with AF and no previous MI, or known or suspected significant structural heart disease, or ventricular scar or fibrosis, use of flecainide3-5 or propafenone5-12 is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm.
3. For patients with AF without recent decompensated HF or severe LV dysfunction, use of dronedarone5,13-15 is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm.

4. For patients with AF without significant baseline QT interval prolongation or uncorrected hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, use of dofetilide1,5,16-17,10,7,18 is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm, with proper dose selection based on kidney function and close monitoring of the QT interval, serum potassium and magnesium concentrations, and kidney function.

5. For patients with AF and normal LV function, use of low-dose amiodarone (100–200 mg/d) is reasonable for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm2,5,17-22 but, in view of its adverse effect profile,5,23,24 should be reserved for patients in whom other rhythm control strategies are ineffective, not preferred, or contraindicated.

6. For patients with AF without significant baseline QT interval prolongation, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, or bradycardia, use of sotalol5-7,10,17,18 may be considered for long-term maintenance of sinus rhythm, with proper dose selection based on kidney function and close monitoring of the QT interval, heart rate, serum potassium and magnesium concentrations, and kidney function.

7. In patients with previous MI and/or significant structural heart disease, including HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), flecainide and propafenone25 should not be administered due to the risk of worsening HF, potential proarrhythmia, and increased mortality.26,27

8. For patients with AF, dronedarone should not be administered for maintenance of sinus rhythm to those with NYHA class III and IV HF or patients who have had an episode of decompensated HF in the past 4 weeks, due to the risk of increased early mortality associated with worsening HF.28

8.4.3. Management of Recurrent AF After Catheter Ablation
content.narrative_summary: The page presents a synopsis explaining that catheter ablation, particularly pulmonary vein isolation (PVI), is an effective rhythm-control strategy for atrial fibrillation (AF) and atrial flutter (AFL). It notes that additional ablation targets beyond PVI have not reduced AF recurrence in randomized trials and that complications may include stroke, transient ischemic attack, pericardial effusion, esophageal atrial fistula, and pulmonary vein stenosis. Supportive text highlights randomized data showing PVI reduces recurrent AF burden versus medical therapy and that various procedural endpoints (e.g., noninducibility, adenosine testing) have mixed predictive value for durable lesion sets.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Techniques and Technologies for AF Catheter Ablation

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients undergoing ablation for AF, PVI is recommended as the primary lesion set for all patients unless a different specific trigger is identified.^1-7

2. In patients undergoing ablation for AF, the value of other endpoints beyond PVI such as noninducibility and ablation of additional anatomic ablation targets (eg, posterior wall sites, low voltage areas, complex fractionated electrograms, rotors) is uncertain.^8-18

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Recurrent AF After Catheter Ablation

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with recurrent symptomatic AF after catheter ablation, repeat catheter ablation or antiarrhythmic drug therapy is useful to improve symptoms and freedom from AF.^1-11

2. In some patients who have undergone catheter ablation of AF, short-term antiarrhythmic drug therapy after ablation can be useful to reduce early recurrences of atrial arrhythmia and hospitalization.^12-16

section_headings: 8.4.4. Anticoagulation Therapy Before and After Catheter Ablation
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis notes that atrial fibrillation (AF) recurs in 30–40% of patients after initial catheter ablation, with 11% requiring repeat ablation within one year; repeat procedures improve symptoms and quality of life but carry risks such as pulmonary vein stenosis and stiff left atrium. Randomized trials demonstrate repeat ablation’s superiority over antiarrhythmic drug therapy for recurrent AF, though head-to-head data are limited. Antiarrhythmic drugs, even if previously ineffective, can decrease recurrent arrhythmias post‐ablation, especially with combined ablation and drug therapy in persistent AF or atrial myopathies. Short‐term (3–6 months) postablation antiarrhythmic therapy reduces early recurrence, and observational data suggest it lowers 90‐day readmissions by 37%.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Anticoagulation Therapy Before and After Catheter Ablation

rows.recommendation: In patients on warfarin who are undergoing catheter ablation of AF, catheter ablation should be performed on uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation with a goal INR of 2.0 to 3.0.
In patients on a DOAC who are undergoing catheter ablation of AF, catheter ablation should be performed with either continuous or minimally interrupted oral anticoagulation.
In patients who have undergone catheter ablation of AF, oral anticoagulation should be continued for at least 3 months after the procedure with a longer duration determined by underlying risk.
In patients who have undergone catheter ablation of AF, continuation of longer-term oral anticoagulation should be dictated according to the patients' stroke risk (eg, CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2).

content.title: 2023 Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis states that catheter ablation reduces arrhythmia burden, improves quality of life, and enhances cardiovascular outcomes, but carries a low risk of stroke (≈0.8% in the first 30 days), underscoring the importance of uninterrupted anticoagulation before, during, and after the procedure. The recommendation-specific supportive text details: (1) all patients require intraprocedural intravenous anticoagulation with heparin or direct thrombin inhibitors, and uninterrupted warfarin is associated with lower thromboembolic and bleeding risks; (2) randomized trials demonstrate that uninterrupted direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are noninferior to uninterrupted warfarin for periprocedural anticoagulation; (3) periprocedural and post-ablation stroke risk due to instrumentation mandates at least two months of continued oral anticoagulation regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc score; and (4) higher atrial fibrillation burden correlates with stroke risk, discontinuation outcomes vary by CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, and ongoing trials (eg, OPTION) are evaluating left atrial appendage occlusion versus continued anticoagulation beyond three months.

section_headings: 8.5. Role of Pacemakers and ICDs for the Prevention and Treatment of AF
content.narrative_summary: Complications of AF catheter ablation occur in approximately 5% of patients, most being vascular. Table 26 details specific complications, including LA-esophageal fistula (0.2%, 1–4 weeks), cardiac perforation with tamponade (0.4%-1.5%, during procedure), CVA/TIA (0.1%-1.0%, during procedure and up to 1 week), PV stenosis (0.1%-0.8%, months), phrenic nerve paralysis (0.2%-0.4%, during procedure), vascular access complications (1%-7%, during procedure up to 1 month), access complications requiring surgery (0.1%-0.3%, during procedure), death (0.1%-0.4%, during procedure), and pneumonia (0.4%-1.0%, days), with associated signs, diagnosis, and treatment. The most severe complication is LA-esophageal fistula. Pericardial tamponade is life-threatening but often treatable with pericardiocentesis. Clinically significant strokes and TIAs occur in <1% of patients. Early PV stenosis was largely due to intravein ablation; antral approaches have made it rare. Bleeding and bruising at vascular access are common; arterial or venous damage or atrioventricular fistula requiring surgery are less common.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the Role of Pacemakers and ICDs for the Prevention and Treatment of AF

rows.recommendation: In patients with bradycardia requiring cardiac-implanted electronic devices who have normal atrioventricular conduction, device selection and programming strategies to maintain atrioventricular synchrony and minimize ventricular pacing should be used to reduce the incidence and progression of AF.
In selected patients with a pacemaker and symptomatic atrial tachyarrhythmias, antitachycardia atrial pacing and ventricular pacing minimization may be useful for reducing symptoms.
In patients with AF who require significant ventricular pacing, conduction system pacing may be useful to reduce progression of AF.
In patients with AF, specialized atrial pacing algorithms designed to suppress AF are not useful for reducing the incidence or slowing the progression of AF.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Surgical Ablation

section_headings: 9.1. General Considerations for AF and HF
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: Among patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) or atrial flutter (AFL), concomitant surgical ablation at the time of cardiac surgery reduces recurrent atrial arrhythmia but increases risk of renal dysfunction and pacemaker placement. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text summarizes historical and contemporary data: the original cut-and-sew atrial maze procedure and subsequent cryoenergy or radiofrequency lesion sets; evidence from Cochrane review and trials demonstrating freedom from AF/AFL/AT versus increased pacemaker placement and renal dysfunction; Virchow’s triad mechanisms underlying thromboembolic risk and protocols recommending oral anticoagulation for at least 3 months post ablation; and a randomized trial of hybrid epicardial plus endocardial ablation showing higher freedom from atrial arrhythmias but increased adverse events. Section 9.1 discusses that AF and heart failure (HF) frequently co-exist, share risk factors and pathophysiology, with higher prevalence of AF in HF and increased mortality associated with AF onset; it refers to Sections 7.2 (specific pharmacological agents for rate control) and 8.2 (electrical and pharmacological cardioversion).

content.title: 9.2. Management of AF in Patients With HF
section_headings: 9.2. Management of AF in Patients With HF
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common cause of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy leading to left ventricular (LV) dysfunction and heart failure (HF), which can be partially or fully reversible with adequate arrhythmia control. AF may be the sole cause of cardiomyopathy or exacerbate LV dysfunction in patients with structural heart disease. It notes that rate and rhythm control therapies in HF have specific safety considerations, and that routine pharmacological rhythm versus rate control has not demonstrated benefit on clinical outcomes.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of AF in Patients With HF

rows.recommendation: In patients who present with a new diagnosis of HFrEF and AF, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy should be suspected, and an early and aggressive approach to AF rhythm control is recommended.1,2

In appropriate patients with AF and HFrEF who are on GDMT, and with reasonable expectation of procedural benefit (Figure 24), catheter ablation is beneficial to improve symptoms, QOL, ventricular function, and cardiovascular outcomes.3-13
In appropriate patients with symptomatic AF and HFpEF with reasonable expectation of benefit, catheter ablation can be useful to improve symptoms and improve QOL.14,15
In patients with AF and HF, digoxin is reasonable for rate control, in combination with other rate-controlling agents or as monotherapy if other agents are not tolerated.16,17

In patients with AF and HF with rapid ventricular rates in whom beta blockers or calcium channel blockers are contraindicated or ineffective, intravenous amiodarone is reasonable for acute rate control.18,19

In patients with AF, HFrEF (LVEF <50%), and refractory rapid ventricular response who are not candidates for or in whom rhythm control has failed, AVNA and biventricular pacing therapy can be useful to improve symptoms, QOL, and EF.20-23

In patients with AF, HF, and implanted biventricular pacing therapy in whom an effective pacing percentage cannot be achieved with pharmacological therapy, AVNA can be beneficial to improve functional class,24,25 reduce the risk of ICD shock,26 and improve survival.24,25

In patients with AF-induced cardiomyopathy who have recovered LV function, long-term surveillance can be beneficial to detect recurrent AF in view of the high risk of recurrence of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.27,28

In patients with suspected AF-induced cardiomyopathy or refractory HF symptoms undergoing pharmacological rate-control therapy for AF, a stricter rate-control strategy (target heart rate <80 bpm at rest and <110 bpm during moderate exercise) may be reasonable.29-31

In patients with AF and HFrEF who undergo AVNA, conduction system pacing of the His bundle or left bundle branch area may be reasonable as an alternative to biventricular pacing to improve symptoms, QOL, and LV function.32-35
In patients with AF and known LVEF <40%, nondihydropyridine calcium channel–blocking drugs should not be administered because of their potential to exacerbate HF.36

For patients with AF, dronedarone should not be administered for maintenance of sinus rhythm to those with NYHA class III and IV HF or patients who have had an episode of decompensated HF in the past 4 weeks, due to the risk of increased early mortality associated with worsening HF.37

content.narrative_summary: Young patients with early-onset AF often have reentrant supraventricular tachycardias treatable by targeted ablation; patients with AF onset before 45 without obvious risk factors may benefit from genetic counseling, testing for rare pathogenic variants, and surveillance for cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia syndromes. In patients with an onset of AF before 45 years of age without obvious risk factors for AF, referral for genetic counseling, genetic testing for rare pathogenic variants, and surveillance for cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia syndromes may be reasonable.

section_headings: 10.3 Management Considerations in Patients With AF and Obesity
10.4 Anticoagulation Considerations in Patients With Class III Obesity
content.narrative_summary: Engaging in moderate levels of exercise has cardiovascular benefits and may lower AF incidence, whereas high-volume endurance exercise (>45 metabolic equivalent-hours/week) is associated with a higher prevalence of AF in young athletes. Mechanisms may involve exercise-induced atrial stretch or inflammation. No prospective studies of detraining exist, but PVI is safe in athletes, improves exercise capacity, and quality of life. Patients with class III obesity (BMI ≥40 kg/m²) are underrepresented in major DOAC trials for AF; post hoc analyses and observational studies show comparable efficacy and safety of DOACs versus warfarin across weight groups, including class III obesity, but limited data exist on pharmacokinetics, efficacy, and safety of DOACs after bariatric surgery.

In patients with AF who have undergone bariatric surgery, warfarin may be reasonable to choose over DOACs for stroke risk reduction in view of concerns about DOAC drug absorption.⁶,⁷

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for ACHD

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults with congenital heart disease and AF, it is recommended to evaluate for and treat precipitating factors and reversible causes of AF, recognizing that residual hemodynamic sequelae may contribute to the occurrence of the arrhythmia.

2. In adults with AF and moderate or complex congenital heart disease, electrophysiological procedures should be performed by operators with expertise in ACHD procedures and in collaboration with an ACHD cardiologist, ideally in specialized centers, when available.

3. In adults with congenital heart disease and symptomatic or hemodynamically significant paroxysmal or persistent AF, an initial strategy of rhythm control is recommended regardless of lesion severity as AF in this population is often poorly tolerated.
4. In symptomatic patients with simple congenital heart disease with antiarrhythmic drug–refractory AF, it is reasonable to choose ablation over long-term antiarrhythmic therapies.

5. In adults with congenital heart disease with AF undergoing PVI, it may be reasonable to include an ablative strategy in the right atrium directed at reentrant arrhythmia secondary to atriotomy scars and the CTI.

6. In adults with AF and moderate or severe forms of congenital heart disease, particularly those with low-flow states such as Fontan circulation, blind-ending cardiac chambers, and cyanosis, it may be reasonable to treat with anticoagulation independent of conventional risk score to reduce risk of thromboembolic events.

content.title: Synopsis
content.narrative_summary: The page provides a synopsis outlining that atrial arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation (AF), are a significant cause of morbidity in adults with congenital heart disease (CHD). Risk factors mirror those in the general population, though an atrial septal defect confers independent risk. CHD is classified as simple, moderate, or complex, guiding pharmacological and ablation strategies that must account for sinus node dysfunction, atrioventricular block, ventricular function, and anatomical considerations requiring operator expertise. The recommendation-specific supportive text presents six key points: 1) evaluate new arrhythmias for treatable causes; 2) specialized ACHD centers yield better procedural outcomes; 3) management of simple CHD follows standard guidelines while therapy for complex CHD must be individualized; 4) AF ablation is safe in simple CHD at experienced centers with anatomy-tailored approaches; 5) PVI has lower success in ACHD and additional ablation targets may be needed, with cryoballoon as an option; 6) all ACHD patients warrant thromboprophylaxis based on individual risk factors, though risk scores may not fully predict events and data on DOACs are limited but promising.

content.title: Prevention and Treatment of AF After Cardiac Surgery
section_headings: 10.9. Prevention and Treatment of AF After Cardiac Surgery
10.9.1. Prevention of AF After Cardiac Surgery
content.narrative_summary: New-onset atrial fibrillation (AF) after cardiac surgery is common and associated with increased risks of late mortality and stroke. Trials of prophylactic amiodarone and beta blockers have variably reduced the occurrence of new AF. The PALACS randomized trial of posterior left pericardiotomy demonstrated a significant reduction in AF (17% versus 32%; P=0.0007; OR 0.44), whereas colchicine showed uncertain benefit and frequent drug discontinuation. Supportive text notes that preoperative beta blockers or amiodarone have shown mixed benefit, with one double-blind RCT of 601 patients demonstrating significant AF reduction with amiodarone, and a meta-analysis and RCT reporting lower incidence of postoperative AF with posterior left pericardiotomy, excluding mitral or tricuspid procedures.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Prevention of AF After Cardiac Surgery

rows.recommendation: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery who are at high risk for postoperative AF, it is reasonable to administer short-term prophylactic beta blockers or amiodarone to reduce the incidence of postoperative AF.
In patients undergoing CABG, aortic valve, or ascending aortic aneurysm operations, it is reasonable to perform concomitant posterior left pericardiotomy to reduce the incidence of postoperative AF.

content.title: 10.9.2. Treatment of AF After Cardiac Surgery
section_headings: 10.9.2. Treatment of AF After Cardiac Surgery
Recommendations for Treatment of AF After Cardiac Surgery
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis discusses that postoperative AF rate control is typically managed with beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers; randomized trials demonstrated no significant difference between rate‐control and rhythm‐control strategies in hemodynamically stable patients. For poorly tolerated or sustained AF, direct current cardioversion with pharmacotherapy and consideration of left appendage imaging if AF persists >48 hours is recommended. Colchicine had shown efficacy but later studies did not confirm benefit and noted gastrointestinal side effects. The recommendation‐specific supportive text provides details on the comparative roles of beta blockers versus calcium channel blockers, the acceptability of rate versus rhythm control, optimal anticoagulation duration (minimum 60 days), timing of rhythm assessment (30–60 days), and the integration of pharmacologic and procedural therapies for postoperative AF.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Treatment of AF After Cardiac Surgery

rows.recommendation: In postoperative cardiac surgery patients, beta blockers* are recommended to achieve rate control for AF1–4 unless contraindicated or ineffective in which case a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker† is recommended.5

In hemodynamically stable cardiac surgery patients with postoperative AF, rate-control (target heart rate, <100 bpm) and/or rhythm-control medications are recommended as initial therapy, with the choice of strategy according to patient symptoms, hemodynamic consequences of the arrhythmia, and physician preference.5,6

In patients who develop poorly tolerated AF after cardiac surgery, direct current cardioversion in combination with antiarrhythmic drug therapy is recommended, with consideration of imaging to rule out left appendage thrombus before cardioversion in those patients in whom AF has been present >48 hours and who have not been on anticoagulation.5,6

In patients who develop postoperative AF after cardiac surgery, it is reasonable to administer anticoagulation when deemed safe in regard to surgical bleeding for 60 days after surgery unless complications develop and to reevaluate the need for longer term anticoagulation at that time.5,7

In patients who develop AF after cardiac surgery and who are treated with rate-control strategy, at 30- to 60-day follow-up it is reasonable to perform rhythm assessment and, if AF does not revert to sinus rhythm spontaneously, consider cardioversion after an adequate duration of anticoagulation.5,6

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes new-onset atrial fibrillation (AF) detected during hospitalization for acute noncardiac illness, noting incidence rates (1–46% in medical illness, 6–22% in severe sepsis, 3–16% after noncardiac surgery) and associations with higher risk of recurrence, prolonged hospitalization, and increased morbidity and mortality. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Pregnancy

rows.recommendation: 1. In pregnant patients with AF, DCCV is safe to the patient and fetus and should be performed in the same manner as in patients who are not pregnant.

2. In pregnant individuals with structurally normal hearts and hemodynamically stable AF, pharmacological cardioversion with agents with history of safe use in pregnancy, such as intravenous procainamide, may be considered.

3. In pregnant individuals with AF and without structural heart disease, antiarrhythmic agents with history of safe use in pregnancy (eg, flecainide and sotalol) are reasonable for maintenance of sinus rhythm.

4. In pregnant individuals with persistent AF, rate-control agents with a record of safety in pregnancy, such as beta blockers (eg, propranolol or metoprolol) and digoxin, either alone or in combination with beta blockers, are reasonable as first-line agents.

5. Pregnant individuals with AF and elevated risk of stroke may be considered for anticoagulation with the recognition that no anticoagulation strategy is completely safe for both the mother and fetus, and an SDM discussion should take place regarding risks to both mother and fetus (Table 28).

content.title: 10.14. Cardio-Oncology and Anticoagulation Considerations
content.narrative_summary: Patients with cancer have a higher incidence of atrial fibrillation (AF) compared to those without cancer, due to shared risk factors, inflammatory and comorbid conditions, tumor cardiac involvement, and certain cancer therapies. New-onset AF in cancer patients is associated with increased risks of heart failure, thromboembolism, bleeding, and mortality. Ibrutinib and other BTK inhibitors carry a notably higher risk of AF. Although cancer patients were underrepresented in DOAC versus VKA trials, observational data suggest similar or lower rates of ischemic stroke and bleeding with DOACs. Careful consideration of drug–drug interactions between cancer therapies, antiarrhythmic agents, and oral anticoagulants is essential.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Cardio-Oncology and Anticoagulation Considerations

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with cancer and AF, multidisciplinary communication including cardiology, oncology and other clinicians, and SDM with the patient is recommended to optimize cancer and AF treatment and to reduce the risk of drug–drug interactions, QTc prolongation, proarrhythmia, bleeding, and thromboembolism.

2. In patients who are to be initiated on cancer therapies associated with an increased risk of developing AF, increased vigilance for incident AF and treatment of contributing factors is reasonable to decrease morbidity.
3. In most patients with AF and cancer (remote history or receiving active cancer treatment), DOACs are reasonable to choose over VKAs for stroke risk reduction.

content.narrative_summary: Certain cancer therapies including anthracyclines, antimetabolites, alkylating agents, immunomodulators, TKIs, VEGF and BRAF inhibitors, CAR T-cell therapy, and monoclonal antibodies are associated with an increased risk of atrial fibrillation. Optimization of cardiovascular risk factors and management of hypertension and heart failure by a cardiologist may decrease incident and recurrent AF and related adverse events in patients starting higher-risk cancer treatments, though specific data in cancer populations are limited. No large randomized trials directly compare DOACs with warfarin in patients with AF and cancer; meta-analyses of post hoc RCTs and observational studies demonstrate that DOACs are associated with lower risks of stroke, systemic embolism, and major bleeding compared with warfarin.

section_headings: 10.16. Anticoagulation Use in Patients With Liver Disease
content.narrative_summary: Post hoc analyses from RCTs comparing DOACs with VKAs demonstrate consistent findings, underscoring the need to consider bleeding risk estimators and antineoplastic drug interactions in AF patients on active cancer treatment. CKD and AF share common risk factors, with CKD associated with higher incident AF and limited AF management data; antiarrhythmic drug dosing should be adjusted based on pharmacokinetics, amiodarone does not require adjustment in CKD, and catheter ablation is feasible with attention to fluid balance. Observational studies comparing OAC therapy versus no OAC in AF patients with active or historical liver disease suggest OACs lower ischemic stroke or thromboembolism risk but increase major bleeding or ICH risk, particularly due to impaired metabolism of factor Xa inhibitors.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Anticoagulation Use in Patients With Liver Disease

rows.recommendation: For patients with AF who are at increased risk of systemic thromboembolism and mild or moderate liver disease (Child-Pugh* class A or B), OAC therapy is reasonable in the absence of clinically significant liver disease–induced coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia.¹–⁷

For patients with AF who are at increased risk of systemic thromboembolism and mild or moderate liver disease (Child-Pugh class A or B) and who are deemed to be candidates for anticoagulation, it is reasonable to prescribe DOACs (Child-Pugh class A: any DOAC; Child-Pugh class B: apixaban, dabigatran, or edoxaban) over warfarin.¹,⁷–¹¹
For patients with AF and moderate liver disease (Child-Pugh class B) at increased risk of systemic thromboembolism, rivaroxaban is contraindicated due to the potentially increased risk of bleeding.¹²
